reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard haematology references
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder of platelet adhesion caused by deficiency or dysfunction of the glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex, the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor
Classic triad is thrombocytopenia, giant platelets on the blood film, and a mucocutaneous bleeding tendency
Because platelets cannot bind von Willebrand factor, they fail to adhere to exposed subendothelium under high shear
Aggregometry shows characteristically absent agglutination to ristocetin that is not corrected by adding normal plasma, while aggregation to other agonists is preserved
Flow cytometry demonstrating reduced surface GPIb (CD42b) distinguishes it from Glanzmann thrombasthenia, where GPIIb/IIIa is deficient
The giant platelets can be miscounted by automated analysers, causing the thrombocytopenia to be overestimated
Management principles include local haemostatic measures, antifibrinolytics, hormonal control of menorrhagia, and platelet transfusion for serious bleeding while minimising alloimmunisation risk
The condition is easily confused with immune thrombocytopenia, so an unnecessary splenectomy or immunosuppression can be avoided by recognising the giant platelets and lifelong history
Recombinant activated factor VII may aid haemostasis in refractory or alloimmunised patients
reference.pathophysiology: Bernard-Soulier syndrome arises from mutations affecting the platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex (subunits GPIbalpha, GPIbbeta and GPIX). This complex is the receptor that binds von Willebrand factor, enabling platelets to adhere to the damaged vessel wall under high shear conditions, the initiating step of primary haemostasis. Loss of functional receptor impairs platelet adhesion and also disrupts normal megakaryocyte fragmentation and platelet membrane structure, producing large, structurally abnormal platelets and a modest thrombocytopenia. The combination of defective adhesion and reduced platelet numbers produces a lifelong bleeding diathesis of variable severity.
additionalDifferentials: Von Willebrand disease (especially type 2B and platelet-type)
Glanzmann thrombasthenia and other platelet function disorders
additionalInvestigations: Blood film to identify giant platelets and confirm true platelet count
Platelet aggregometry showing absent ristocetin-induced agglutination not corrected by normal plasma
Flow cytometry for platelet GPIb-IX-V complex (CD42a/CD42b)
Von Willebrand studies to exclude platelet-type and type 2B VWD
Molecular genetic testing of GP1BA, GP1BB and GP9
redFlags: Severe or life-threatening haemorrhage (gastrointestinal or intracranial bleeding)
Bleeding unresponsive to platelet transfusion suggesting alloimmunisation
Planned surgery or delivery without a defined haemostatic plan
reference.prognosis: Most patients have a near-normal life expectancy with supportive management, though bleeding episodes can be serious and occasionally life-threatening. Recurrent mucosal bleeding, menorrhagia and the risk of platelet alloimmunisation are the principal long-term concerns.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the condition as immune thrombocytopenia and giving inappropriate immunosuppression or splenectomy
Relying on automated platelet counts that undercount giant platelets
Transfusing platelets unnecessarily and provoking alloimmunisation
Using antiplatelet drugs or NSAIDs that worsen bleeding
Neglecting iron replacement for chronic blood loss
management: Manage bleeding with local haemostatic measures and antifibrinolytics such as tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeds and minor procedures
Reserve platelet transfusion for major bleeding or surgery, using HLA-matched leucodepleted products to limit alloimmunisation
Consider recombinant activated factor VII for bleeding refractory to platelet support or where alloimmunisation has occurred
Control menorrhagia with antifibrinolytics and hormonal therapy such as the combined oral contraceptive or a levonorgestrel intrauterine system
Avoid antiplatelet drugs including aspirin and NSAIDs, and maintain iron supplementation for chronic blood loss
Undertake pre-procedure haematology planning and ensure hepatitis B immunisation given transfusion exposure
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder with screening of at-risk relatives
